questions.q: How does the summary describe life with clinical anxiety?
a: A constant, draining battle that limits ordinary activities
A brief reaction that fades after a stressful event
A problem that only appears during major life crises
A habit that gradually disappears with age
questions.why: Lesson 1 compares the daily struggle to managing diabetes and describes limits like avoiding public places.

questions.q: Why do ordinary fears of snakes or heights still exist, according to the summary?
a: They helped our ancestors survive and still protect us
They are learned from anxious parents in childhood
They come from watching frightening films as children
They are early signs of clinical anxiety disorder
questions.why: Lesson 2 traces common fears to evolution: avoiding cliffs and snakes helped ancestors live longer.

questions.q: What did research on rhesus monkeys suggest about anxiety?
a: Separation from a parent can raise anxiety later in life
Anxiety is passed down only through genes
Monkeys raised alone grow into calmer adults
Parenting style has no measurable effect on anxiety
questions.why: Lesson 2 cites young monkeys separated from their mothers who showed more anxiety, social problems and aggression later.

questions.q: What does exposure therapy ask patients to do?
a: Face what they fear in order to get past it
Avoid the feared situation until panic fades
Discuss childhood memories without facing the fear
Take medication before every stressful event
questions.why: Lesson 3 describes exposure therapy, the most widely used form of CBT, as confronting the feared thing directly.

questions.q: Why can medication help someone with clinical anxiety?
a: It can address the brain's difficulty producing serotonin
It permanently rewires the brain's fear circuits
It removes any need for talking therapy
It works identically for every anxious person
questions.why: Lesson 3 explains that anxious brains often struggle to produce serotonin, and drugs can help correct this.
